title: Will German Rearmament Save Europe?
gist: Reviewing Liana Fix's 'Germany Rearmed', Lazard's Theodore Bunzel argues German rearmament (doubled spending, 649 billion euros planned for 2025-29, outspending France and the U.K. combined by 2029) is Europe's indispensable backbone but must be 'Europeanized' to avoid fragmentation and AfD risk; he disputes Fix's view that U.S. disengagement is permanent and urges Europe to build complementary capabilities rather than replace U.S. enablers.

themes.theme: Size and trajectory of European/German defense spending

insights.claim: European defense spending nearly doubled in real terms in six years, from 242 billion euros in 2020 to 454 billion euros in 2026.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Structural multi-year demand for European defense contractors.
insights.quote: from 242 billion euros in 2020 to 454 billion euros in 2026
insights.locator: Old assumptions, however, are finally changing.

insights.claim: If Europe meets NATO's target of 3.5 percent of GDP on defense by 2035 (versus little more than 2 percent today), the annual spending surge will rival the Marshall Plan relative to Europe's GDP.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Implies a decade-long fiscal impulse comparable to postwar reconstruction; supports defense equities and higher Euro-area bond supply.
insights.quote: the surge in annual spending will rival the scale of the Marshall Plan relative to Europe’s GDP
insights.locator: Old assumptions, however, are finally changing.

insights.claim: Germany has doubled defense spending since 2021, accounting for more than a quarter of the EU's increase, and on current budgets will spend more on its military by 2029 than France and the U.K. spend combined today.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: German defense primes are the main beneficiaries of European rearmament.
insights.quote: by 2029, Germany will spend more on its military than France and the U.K. today spend combined
insights.locator: As Council on Foreign Relations scholar Liana Fix

insights.claim: Germany plans to spend a total of 649 billion euros on defense between 2025 and 2029, reaching 3.5 percent of GDP annually, up from 1.15 percent in 2015.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Hard budget numbers anchor revenue visibility for German and European defense suppliers through 2029.
insights.quote: Between 2025 and 2029, Germany plans to spend a total of 649 billion euros
insights.locator: Only in 2025, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz

insights.claim: Germany is one of the few European countries with fiscal headroom to rearm, with a 64 percent debt-to-GDP ratio while French bond markets are 'quaking', and its economy is a third larger than the U.K.'s and 50 percent larger than France's.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Fiscal capacity divergence: Bund issuance funds defense while French spreads remain a stress point.
insights.quote: With French bond markets quaking, Germany is one of the only countries with the fiscal headroom to spend, with a debt-to-GDP ratio of 64 percent.
insights.locator: And Germany is undoubtedly the most consequential

insights.claim: Kiel Institute estimates suggest defense spending could raise European productivity growth by 0.25 percent per 1 percent of GDP spent, if focused on R&D and equipment rather than pensions and personnel, making rearmament a rare growth bright spot.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Composition of spending matters: R&D/equipment-heavy budgets favor tech-oriented defense and dual-use firms.
insights.quote: may boost sagging European productivity growth by 0.25 percent per every 1 percent of GDP spent on defense
insights.locator: It’s a remarkable feature of our turbulent era

themes.theme: Trump, not Putin, as Germany's real catalyst

insights.claim: Fix convincingly credits Trump's return to the White House, more than Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, as the real catalyst for German rearmament; Scholz's 100 billion euro Zeitenwende fund was slow to disburse and not followed by bold moves.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: European defense spending is driven by U.S. reliability doubts, so it should persist even if the Ukraine war ends.
insights.quote: history had to repeat itself twice for Germany to abandon the ‘myth of pacifism’ and to seriously begin rearmament.

insights.claim: Germany's 'myth of pacifism' is overstated: West German defense spending exceeded 3 percent of GDP through the mid-1970s, and the Bundeswehr fought in the Balkans and Afghanistan, where it lost 55 soldiers.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Historical precedent shows 3%+ German defense budgets are politically sustainable.
insights.locator: But Fix provides nuance to this myth

insights.claim: German public opinion has shifted: fall 2024 polling showed 73 percent wanted more investment in European security and 65 percent supported a defense target of 3 percent of GDP or higher.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Broad public support lowers political risk of defense-budget reversal.

insights.claim: Germany's economy is roughly twice Russia's and the EU's nearly 10 times, giving Europe with Germany as backbone the overwhelming means to check a revanchist Russia.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Europe's constraint is will and coordination, not resources.

themes.theme: Risk of nationalized rearmament fragmenting Europe

insights.claim: German rearmament has so far been largely national, with spending at the German level and funding going mostly to German defense firms, risking fragmentation of European military production and suspicion from France, Poland, and Central/Eastern European neighbors.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Near-term contract flow favors German national champions over pan-European consolidation.
insights.locator: But what kind of military power will Germany be?

insights.claim: Fix's solution, endorsed by Bunzel, is to 'Europeanize' German rearmament: European-level spending on shared platforms, an integrated European command, and a continent-wide defense-industrial base, which would also constrain a future AfD government.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Watch for joint EU procurement and funding vehicles as policy signals benefiting cross-border defense consortia.
insights.locator: Fix’s solution, which is a compelling one

insights.claim: The AfD leads every German national poll, averaging 29 percent versus the CDU/CSU's 19 percent, and advocates 5 percent of GDP defense spending with an affinity for Russia and China, though its path to power before 2029 elections remains narrow due to the firewall.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Long-tail political risk to German policy direction; an AfD-led Germany would control one of the world's most powerful militaries.
insights.quote: The AfD now leads every national poll in Germany, averaging 29 percent to the Christian Democratic Union/Christian Socialist Union’s 19 percent.
insights.locator: The greater threat to European security

insights.claim: France's far-right National Rally appears poised to win the French presidency in the spring, raising questions about how a right-wing France would affect European rearmament.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: A National Rally presidency is a 2027 event risk for French bonds and EU defense integration.
insights.quote: which appears poised to win the French presidency in the spring
insights.locator: However unlikely an AfD-run Germany may be

themes.theme: U.S. role: reconciliation, not permanent divorce

insights.claim: Bunzel disputes Fix's view that Washington is 'never going back' and that trans-Atlantic ties will become patron-client; after Republicans' midterm drubbing and given Trump's idiosyncratic favoritism toward Russia and China, he sees higher odds of U.S.-European reconciliation after 2029.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing a full U.S. exit from NATO; Article V commitment likely persists.
insights.quote: a patron-client relationship more than an alliance, with no preferred treatment for Europeans.
insights.locator: The question of Washington’s future role

insights.claim: Bunzel predicts Europe will barrel into a trade conflict with Beijing over surging Chinese exports in coming years, creating shared interests with Washington.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Expect rising EU trade defense measures against Chinese imports (e.g., tariffs, anti-dumping).
insights.locator: This likely over-indexes on the wrecking ball

insights.claim: Replacing core U.S. enablers like space-based intelligence and integrated air and missile defense would cost more than $1 trillion per the IISS and take up to a decade, so Europe should instead build complementary capacity in ground forces, missiles, unmanned systems, and munitions while relying on the U.S. nuclear umbrella.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Points spending toward munitions, missiles, drones, and land systems as the most likely European procurement priorities.
insights.quote: The International Institute for Strategic Studies puts the cost of fully replacing US capabilities at more than $1 trillion.
insights.locator: This matters because it should inform

insights.claim: Roughly 80,000 U.S. troops remain in Europe 75 years after Eisenhower said U.S. forces should be only a temporary bridge, showing Europe never fully shouldered its own defense.
insights.speaker: Theodore Bunzel
insights.so_what: Baseline for tracking gradual U.S. troop drawdowns.
insights.locator: Ike’s forecast, it seems, was wrong
